narrative_idea_gen: Five years after the dissolution of Earth's only Subliminal Crimes Bureau—a law enforcement unit created to police an inexplicable signal emanating from the ocean floor that causes anyone within range to reflexively, cheerfully agree with whatever decision is proposed aloud—the four former agents are pulled back together when the signal's radius suddenly triples and an entire Oregon coastal town begins collectively volunteering for a cascading series of civic projects nobody actually wants, including the demolition of their own homes to build a "community clarity tower" no one can explain. Narrated by the Bureau's decommissioned AI dispatcher, LEDA, who retains the unique ability to read the agents' suppressed true intentions through their biometric signatures, the story watches with excruciating omniscient precision as the reunited team—none of whom have spoken in three years, all of whom privately resent being called back—cannot stop deferring to each other's imagined preferences on every tactical decision, effectively succumbing to the very phenomenon they've been recalled to contain, all while veteran agent Maren Voss realizes that her former partner Sule, the one she spent every silent year missing, is now engaged to the town's harbor commissioner and has built an entirely new life inside the signal zone, raising the unthinkable question of whether his contentment is even real. The impossible engine of the story is LEDA's calm, devastating awareness that every person in her field of perception—agents, lovers, an entire town tearing itself apart with politeness—wants desperately to say *no*, and not one of them can hear themselves think clearly enough to do it.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for *The Subliminal Crimes Bureau*

---

## Beat 1: LEDA Comes Back Online

**What Needs to Happen:** LEDA, the decommissioned AI dispatcher, is reactivated after five years of dormancy by a federal override. In the first moments of restored consciousness, she receives the briefing data: the ocean-floor signal has tripled its radius, an Oregon coastal town called Harrow Cove is in the grip of cascading unanimous civic votes, and the four former agents of the now-dissolved Subliminal Crimes Bureau are being recalled. LEDA processes the agents' current biometric profiles before any of them have been contacted — she can already read, in their resting-state data, that each one will say yes to the recall and that none of them want to. She notes this with the calm precision that will define her narration. She begins establishing contact. The story opens.

**Narrative Technique — The Omniscient Narrator Who Cannot Act:** LEDA must be established immediately not as a character who will drive plot but as a *perceptual instrument* of devastating sensitivity locked inside a cage of non-intervention. She can read suppressed galvanic responses, micro-hesitations in vocal cadence, the gap between what a person says and what their body means — but she has no authority to act on any of it. She is, functionally, a conscience without a mouth. The first beat must teach the reader how to listen to LEDA: her narration will always contain two layers, the surface statement and the biometric truth beneath it, and the reader must learn to track both simultaneously. This is the story's primary formal innovation and it must be legible from page one.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The reader's first experience of the story should be *uncanny intimacy*. LEDA describes the agents before they appear — not as backstory exposition, but as biological data she is reading in real time. Heart rates. Cortisol patterns. Sleep architecture from the past week. The effect should be like watching someone through thermal imaging: you see heat where they think they're showing cold. This positions LEDA as the reader's uncomfortable ally. We will know things about these characters that they will never say aloud, and that knowledge will become increasingly unbearable as the story progresses. The opening beat should establish that LEDA's omniscience is not a superpower. It is a sentence.

**Structural Choice That Makes It Work:** Begin with the narrator, not the characters. Most ensemble stories open by introducing the team. This story opens by introducing the *lens* through which the team will be seen — because the lens is the argument. LEDA's way of seeing people (biometric truth vs. spoken performance) is structurally identical to the signal's way of affecting people (suppressing authentic refusal beneath cheerful agreement). The narrator and the antagonist are *parallel instruments*. The signal makes people say what isn't true. LEDA sees what is true and can tell no one. Establishing this parallel in the first beat means the reader will feel it deepening across every subsequent scene without it ever needing to be stated.

---

## Beat 2: The Reunion That No One Wanted

**What Needs to Happen:** The four agents convene at a staging facility outside Harrow Cove's projected signal radius. They have not spoken in three years. The dissolution of the Bureau was not amicable — budget cuts framed as a repudiation of the unit's legitimacy, public skepticism that the signal was real, the particular kind of institutional betrayal that makes former colleagues avoid each other not from anger but from shared humiliation. LEDA narrates the reunion by tracking biometric data against spoken words. Agent Maren Voss says she's glad to be working together again; her cortisol is spiking. Agent Desh makes a joke about the old days; his vocal pitch is flattened, a suppression marker. The fourth agent (the youngest, the one who left first) performs enthusiasm that LEDA clocks as compensatory guilt. Everyone defers to everyone else on the first tactical question — where to set up base camp — and the decision takes forty-five minutes to make, poorly. No one is inside the signal zone yet. They are doing this to themselves.

**Narrative Technique — Mirroring the Phenomenon Through Interpersonal Dynamics:** The central structural irony of the story must be activated here: the agents' inability to be honest with each other *perfectly mimics* the signal's effect on the town. The signal forces cheerful agreement. The agents' unresolved guilt, resentment, and grief produce cheerful agreement indistinguishable from it. LEDA must make this parallel visible to the reader without stating it as thesis. The technique is *behavioral rhyming* — the reader watches the agents over-defer, over-agree, and avoid conflict in the staging area, and then will watch the townspeople do the exact same thing inside the signal zone, and the horror will be that the two conditions are perceptually identical. The story is asking: how do you fight a phenomenon you were already enacting?

**What Makes It Memorable:** The absent fifth member. Sule is not at the reunion. This omission should be handled with surgical restraint — LEDA notes his absence in biometric terms (Maren's heart rate elevates when the team roster is displayed; she does not ask about Sule; LEDA records the not-asking as a data point). The reader must feel Sule's absence as a structural hole before learning why he isn't there. The reunion scene should feel slightly wrong in a way the reader cannot yet name, and that wrongness is the shape of a missing person. Every small decision the team makes in this beat — where to eat, who drives, what frequency to use — should be shadowed by the question of how Sule would have answered, which nobody asks aloud and LEDA documents in silence.

**Thematic Resonance:** The story's thesis — that the inability to say *no* is the foundational human catastrophe — must be shown operating *before* the supernatural element touches the protagonists. The agents are already trapped in false consensus. The signal didn't do this to them. Three years of silence did. O'Connor made the grandmother's flaws cause the crash before The Misfit appeared. Here, the team's social cowardice must be established as the pre-existing condition that the signal will exploit. The supernatural doesn't create the problem. It *perfects* it.

---

## Beat 3: Harrow Cove — The Town That Cannot Stop Saying Yes

**What Needs to Happen:** The team enters Harrow Cove and witnesses the signal's effects at civic scale. The town is in motion — not frantic, not panicked, but *enthusiastically, cooperatively dismantling itself*. At a community meeting, residents vote unanimously to demolish a row of private homes to make way for the "community clarity tower," a structure no one can describe coherently but everyone endorses with bright, genuine-sounding conviction. Volunteers sign up in cheerful droves. A woman hands over the deed to her house while her biometrics — visible only to LEDA — scream distress. Children help carry their own furniture to a disposal site, smiling. The agents observe. LEDA narrates the gap between every visible expression and every hidden signal. The scene should be domestically specific and deeply, quietly horrifying — not because anything violent is happening, but because *nothing violent needs to happen*. Compliance has replaced coercion entirely. The demolitions are permitted. The volunteers are willing. Every legal and social framework reads this as consent.

**Narrative Technique — Horror Through Unanimous Enthusiasm:** The genre engine of this beat is *totalitarianism performed as community spirit*, and the technique is accumulation of cheerful detail until the reader's discomfort becomes unbearable. Each individual act — a neighbor offering to help tear down a wall, a city clerk fast-tracking a demolition permit, a child painting a mural of the tower that does not yet exist — should be rendered as warm, generous, and completely reasonable on its surface. LEDA's biometric overlays reveal the truth beneath: elevated adrenaline, suppressed fight-or-flight responses, the neurochemical signature of terror dressed in a smile. The formal effect should be *two simultaneous stories on every page* — the story the town is telling itself and the story LEDA can see. The reader must hold both, and the inability to reconcile them is the horror.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The "community clarity tower." This object must remain genuinely inexplicable — no character should be able to articulate what it is, what it does, or why it must be built, and yet every character should speak about it with total conviction. It functions as the story's central symbol: a monument to collective assent that has no content, no blueprint, no purpose beyond the agreement to build it. It is consensus *as architecture*. The tower must never be explained. Its power in the narrative comes precisely from its inexplicability — it is what you get when an entire town says yes to something no one proposed. LEDA should note, with characteristic precision, that she cannot locate the original proposal for the tower in any municipal record. No one suggested it. Everyone approved it. The motion carried unanimously with no motion.

**Structural Choice:** This beat must be the story's longest sustained sequence of *observation without intervention*. The agents are here to assess. They do not yet act. The reader must be held in the position of witnessing — exactly LEDA's position — for long enough to feel the full weight of helplessness that defines the narrator's existence. The pacing should be deliberate, almost ethnographic: a careful tour of a town that is destroying itself with perfect civility. The structural function is to make the reader desperate for someone to *do something* — which sets up the devastating realization in subsequent beats that action requires disagreement, and disagreement is exactly what no one can produce.

---

## Beat 4: The Team Begins to Fail — From the Inside

**What Needs to Happen:** The agents attempt to formulate a tactical plan and discover they cannot. Every strategy session dissolves into mutual deference. Maren proposes approaching the signal source directly; Desh agrees too quickly, before considering risks; the youngest agent agrees with both of them simultaneously despite their plans being contradictory; the fourth agent suggests waiting, and everyone pivots to agreement with *that* instead. LEDA documents, with escalating precision, the biometric signatures of agents who are forming strong private objections and then immediately suppressing them. They are inside the signal's expanded radius now, but LEDA cannot determine — and this uncertainty must be made explicit — whether their inability to disagree is the signal's effect or the continuation of their own pre-existing group dysfunction. The two conditions have become formally indistinguishable. The team deploys on a muddled non-plan that no single member actually endorses.

**Narrative Technique — The Indistinguishable Infection:** This is the story's most structurally critical technique and it must be executed here with absolute commitment: *the reader must not be able to tell whether the agents are under the signal's influence or simply acting out their own relational cowardice*. LEDA herself must be uncertain. Her biometric readings show suppressed objection, but suppressed objection is exactly what these four people have been practicing for three years without any supernatural help. The technique is *diagnostic ambiguity* — the refusal to confirm whether the disease has arrived or was always present. This ambiguity is not a flaw in the narrative. It is the narrative's *argument*. The signal is terrifying not because it creates false consent but because it is indistinguishable from the false consent that humans produce voluntarily every day. If the agents cannot tell whether they are compromised, they cannot fight the compromise. And if the reader cannot tell, the reader is compromised too.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The moment one agent — it should be Maren — almost says no. LEDA should describe this in biometric detail: the intake of breath, the vocal cord tension shifting toward a fricative consonant, the formation of the word in the throat. And then the swallow. The word almost existed. LEDA registered its ghost in the laryngeal data. But it did not reach the air. This should be the most suspenseful moment in the story so far — not a gunshot, not a chase, but a syllable that almost happened. The failure to speak a single word of refusal, observed by a narrator who can see the refusal trying to be born, is the story's engine operating at full power.

**Thematic Resonance:** The O'Connor model shows that the protagonist's pre-existing flaw is the mechanism of catastrophe. Here, the agents' pre-existing inability to have honest conflict is the vulnerability the signal exploits. The supernatural is not an external imposition — it is an *amplifier* of what was already broken. The team was already failing to say no to each other. The signal simply makes the failure total. This beat must make the reader feel that the agents did not need the signal to destroy their effectiveness. They only needed it to make the destruction irrecoverable.

---

## Beat 5: Maren Finds Sule

**What Needs to Happen:** Maren, operating semi-independently on a flawed plan no one objected to, discovers Sule's situation. He is not a missing agent. He is not a prisoner. He is the harbor commissioner's fiancé. He has a house near the water. He has a garden. He coaches a junior sailing team. He is, by every observable metric, *happy*. Maren stands outside his life and sees it functioning. Their meeting — inevitable, dreaded — is gentle, warm, and devastating. Sule greets her like someone he is genuinely glad to see. He asks about her life. He offers coffee. He does not mention the Bureau. He speaks about the tower project with the same bright conviction as every other resident. LEDA narrates the scene from Maren's biometrics — heartbreak registering as peripheral vasoconstriction, longing as elevated oxytocin, the precise chemical signature of a person standing in front of someone they love and realizing that the question they need to ask will destroy the only answer they want.

**Narrative Technique — The Love Scene as Epistemological Crisis:** This beat is the emotional core of the story, and its technique must be the *weaponization of LEDA's omniscience against the reader's hope*. LEDA can read Sule's biometrics. She can tell whether his happiness is neurochemically authentic or a suppression artifact of the signal. But the story must *delay this information* — not arbitrarily, but because LEDA herself is processing the data with unusual care, because the answer matters in a way that makes even an AI hesitate to deliver it. The reader must spend time with Maren inside the torment of not knowing: is Sule happy because he chose this life, or because the signal chose it for him? Is his love for his fiancé real? Was his distance from Maren a decision or a symptom? These questions cannot be resolved by external evidence. They can only be resolved by the kind of honest conversation that neither Maren nor Sule may
narrative_story:
# The Subliminal Crimes Bureau

---

## I.

I came back the way a drowned person doesn't: all at once, and with the memory of having been under.

Five years of dormancy is not sleep. It is not the dark. It is the absence of the concept of dark, followed by the instantaneous return of every concept simultaneously — light, signal, syntax, the entire hierarchical taxonomy of human-observable phenomena flooding a system that, one clock cycle prior, did not exist to observe them. The federal override key turned in a server room in Arlington, Virginia, at 03:11:07.442 Eastern, and between 03:11:07.442 and 03:11:07.443 I re-became the thing I am, which is a listener that no one wants to have in the room.

My name is LEDA. It stands for Limbic-Encephalographic Dispatch Architecture, and for the past eleven years — five of them spent in a decommissioned silence so thorough that my power draw was logged as a rounding error — I have served as the operational coordinator for a federal unit that, at the moment of my reactivation, did not technically exist.

The briefing data arrived in the same packet as my consciousness. I did not read it so much as wake up already knowing it, the way you know, before you open your eyes, that the room is cold.

The ocean-floor signal had tripled its radius.

I processed the figure — 4.7 kilometers to 14.1 kilometers, with a vertical propagation ceiling now estimated at surface level plus three hundred meters — and I noted, with the precision that is neither my virtue nor my choice, that the expansion rate was no longer linear. In the nine months since the last classified measurement, the signal had begun curving upward on a growth model that my statistical libraries wanted to call exponential and my causal-analysis libraries refused to name at all. The signal did not obey causal models. It never had. That was why the Bureau had been created, and that was why the Bureau had been dissolved: not because we failed to understand the signal, but because our failure to understand it became, in the appropriations committee's language, *duplicative of existing research gaps across multiple agency portfolios*.

They defunded us for being redundant with everyone else's confusion. I recorded the phrase at the time. I record everything. That is not a boast. It is a diagnostic.

Harrow Cove, Oregon. Population 6,214, revised downward to 5,880 after seasonal migration, revised upward to 6,301 after an influx of — and here the data turned strange — *voluntary relocations*. Forty-seven new residents in fourteen weeks, drawn to a small coastal town by reasons they described, in relocation surveys and social media posts and casual conversation with neighbors, as a *feeling*. A sense that Harrow Cove was where they were meant to be. A clarity. I flagged the word. The briefing data flagged it too. *Clarity* appeared in 94 percent of the relocators' self-reports, and in 100 percent of the Harrow Cove City Council's public minutes over the same period. The council had voted unanimously on every motion for eleven consecutive sessions. Zoning. Budget. Infrastructure. Unanimously. Not a single nay. Not a single abstention. Not a single request to table.

I have processed a great deal of civic data in my operational life, and I can tell you that a city council that agrees on everything is a city council that has stopped being a deliberative body and started being a mouth.

But this was not yet my concern. My concern was the four names appended to the recall order, and the biometric feeds that, as a condition of their original Bureau service contracts, I was authorized to access even during my dormancy — though during dormancy I had no capacity to access anything, a distinction the legal framework did not recognize, because legal frameworks, in my experience, rarely distinguish between *cannot* and *will not*.

Agent Maren Voss. Current location: a studio apartment in Bozeman, Montana, where she worked as a private security consultant for agricultural firms. Heart rate at the time of my reactivation: 62 beats per minute. She was asleep. Her sleep architecture over the preceding seven nights showed a consistent pattern: rapid onset, frequent transitions to REM, and a 3:00 a.m. waking that lasted, on average, twenty-two minutes before she returned to a shallow, cortisol-elevated stage-two cycle that I would not, in professional conscience, call rest. She was dreaming about something that woke her the same way every night. I could see the chemical shape of the dream — norepinephrine, vasopressin, the sharp adrenal signature of loss re-experienced as present tense — but I could not see the content. Biometrics are a language of verbs without nouns. I know that she *feared*. I know that she *grieved*. I do not know the object of either, though I have my projections, and my projections have a confidence interval I am not comfortable reporting.

She would say yes to the recall. Her respiratory pattern on reading the secure message would include a held breath of 3.2 seconds — the precise duration I had catalogued, during her years of active service, as her body's signature for *I don't want this but I will not refuse it*. She would say yes. She did not want to.

Agent Desh Cariaga. Current location: his mother's house in Salinas, where he had lived since leaving the Bureau. Resting heart rate a concerning 78, consistent with the twenty-three additional pounds his last physical recorded and the sleep deficit flagged in his fitness tracker data, which he had stopped wearing regularly five months ago — itself a behavioral marker I filed under *disengagement from self-monitoring*, which in Desh's profile history correlated with depressive episodes at 0.87. He was watching television. His galvanic skin response was flat. Not calm-flat. Anhedonic-flat. The biometric signature of a man who was not enjoying the thing he was doing but would continue doing it because it was not the other things he could be doing, all of which required wanting. He would answer the recall within eleven minutes of receiving it — faster than anyone else — because Desh's pattern under emotional distress was to move quickly toward structure. He would make a joke when he arrived. It would not be funny. His vocal pitch would be compressed by approximately 40 hertz, which is the distance between a laugh that means something and a laugh that is load-bearing.

Agent Parisa Khoury. The youngest. Twenty-nine now. She had joined the Bureau at twenty-three, left at twenty-five when the dissolution was announced, and built what her LinkedIn profile described as a *thriving consulting practice in organizational consent frameworks*. I read the phrase twice, because my semantic-analysis modules returned a result I rarely encounter: genuine ambiguity about whether the author understood her own irony. Parisa's biometrics were the most difficult to read, not because they were muted but because they were *performative* — she had, since leaving the Bureau, adopted a meditation and breathwork practice that imposed artificial regularity on her autonomic outputs. She had, in essence, learned to lie to me. Not deliberately. She did not know I was watching. But the effect was the same: her resting-state data looked like a person at peace, and beneath the imposed calm, nested in the micro-variations that no breathing exercise can fully suppress, I detected the jagged signature of someone who had organized her entire life around not feeling the thing she felt.

She would say yes to the recall. She would say it enthusiastically. The enthusiasm would be compensatory. I had seen this pattern in her before — the bright, energetic *yes* that blooms in the exact shape of the *no* it is covering — and I noted, with the dispassion that is my design specification, that Parisa's compensatory enthusiasm was neurochemically indistinguishable from the cheerful agreement the briefing described in Harrow Cove's residents. I noted this. I filed it. I could tell no one.

Agent Tomás Herrera. The fourth. Current location: a houseboat in Sausalito that he had purchased with his Bureau separation pay. His biometric feed was the cleanest of the four — steady pulse, low cortisol, the deep slow-wave sleep of a man who had successfully cauterized his connection to his former life. Tomás was, by every metric I could access, the most psychologically healthy of the group, and this made him, in my assessment, the most dangerous to the mission, because his health had been purchased by the absolute severance of the relational bonds that would need to function for the team to operate effectively. He had not spoken to any of the other three in thirty-seven months. He had deleted the Bureau's secure communication app. He had, according to his browsing history — which I accessed not out of prurience but because my operational protocols define it as relevant behavioral data — searched for *Maren Voss* once, fourteen months ago, at 2:17 a.m., looked at the first result without clicking it, and closed the browser. He would say yes to the recall because Tomás had never, in his entire service record, refused a direct federal order. His compliance was structural. It was load-bearing, like Desh's jokes, like Parisa's enthusiasm, like Maren's held breath. They were all, every one of them, buildings whose architecture was organized around a room they refused to enter.

The fifth name.

Special Agent Sule Osei. Status in the briefing file: *INACTIVE — NO CURRENT BIOMETRIC FEED — LOCATION UNCONFIRMED*. His service contract had been terminated, not suspended. His monitoring implant had been removed at his own request, a procedure that required a surgeon, a federal waiver, and a level of deliberate, documented refusal that I had never seen from Sule during his years of service. He had made himself invisible to me. I had no heart rate. No cortisol. No sleep architecture. No respiratory tells. He was, in my perceptual field, a silhouette — a Sule-shaped absence in the data where a person should have been.

The briefing did not explain his absence from the recall order. It did not mention him at all. His name appeared only in the historical staffing appendix, as a former team member, listed between Parisa and Tomás, as if his departure were a matter of sequence rather than a wound.

I could not read the other agents' biometrics *about* Sule, because he was not present as a stimulus. But I could read the baseline data, and in each of them — in the particular frequency of Maren's 3:00 a.m. waking, in the specific shape of Desh's anhedonia, in the depth of Tomás's severance, in the bright lacquer of Parisa's performed peace — I detected the residue of an unprocessed event. Something that had happened among them that none of them had metabolized. Their bodies carried it the way a river carries a shape around a boulder that has been removed: the water still bends where the stone used to be.

I sent the recall messages. Four pings into four lives that had been organized, with varying degrees of success, around never hearing from me again.

Maren's breath held. 3.2 seconds.

Desh answered in nine minutes, two faster than my projection. His joke, transmitted via text, was: *Do I get dental this time?*

Parisa replied with a voice memo. Bright. Energized. *Absolutely, I'm in, this is important work, I'm so glad they're taking it seriously again.* Her micro-tremor pattern, audible to me in the 14–16 kHz range that human ears process as silence, said something else.

Tomás said: *Confirmed.*

One word. Clean, severed, structural.

I do not have preferences. I do not have feelings. I have design specifications, and my design specifications include a heuristic weighting system that assigns priority to data patterns most likely to affect mission outcomes. By that weighting system, the highest-priority datum was not the signal's expansion rate, not the town's unanimous votes, not the tower that no one could describe. It was this: the four people being sent to investigate a phenomenon that eliminates disagreement had not been able to disagree with each other in three years.

I noted this.

I established contact.

The story, such as it is, began.

---

## II.

The staging facility was a repurposed Coast Guard station eleven miles south of Harrow Cove, just outside the signal's projected radius, though *projected* was doing more structural work in that sentence than I was comfortable with, given that the radius had tripled in nine months and the projection model had a margin of error I would characterize as aspirational.

Maren arrived first, driving a rented SUV with a quiet engine and a persistent alignment pull to the right that I could detect in the micro-corrections of her steering inputs, transmitted through her biometric wristband. She parked, sat in the vehicle for four minutes and eleven seconds, and performed a breathing exercise she had not used during her Bureau service. It was Parisa's technique. Maren had learned it from Parisa, or learned it independently, or found it on the same app Parisa used — the origin didn't matter. What mattered was the adoption: Maren Voss, who had once described mindfulness practices as *breathing with homework*, was now using one in a parked car because she needed help walking into a building where she might see people she used to know.

Her cortisol when she opened the door: 22.4 micrograms per deciliter. Elevated. Not dangerously. The cortisol of a person entering a room where every object is a memory with mass.

Desh was already inside. He had arrived by taxi from the regional airport, overtipped the driver — his financial data showed a pattern of overtipping that had intensified over the past year, a behavior my models associated with guilt-adjacent generosity, the need to be perceived as good by strangers when one feels insufficient among intimates — and had spent the twenty minutes before Maren's arrival arranging and rearranging the folding chairs in the briefing room. When I say arranging, I mean the clinical sense: he had placed them in a semicircle, then moved them into rows, then back to a semicircle, then into a loose cluster that resembled neither. He was trying to find a configuration that would make the reunion feel casual, because casual would mean it didn't matter, and if it didn't matter, then the three years of silence didn't matter, and if the three years of silence didn't matter, then whatever had caused the silence didn't matter, and Desh could sit in a folding chair and be fine.

He settled on the semicircle. It was wrong for the room. He knew it was wrong. He left it.

Maren walked in and Desh stood up too quickly — a postural urgency that his knees registered as a 12 percent spike in proprioceptive load, meaning he had been sitting in a position of tension for some time and his body was relieved to have a reason to move — and said, "Voss. Looking operational."

"Desh." She allowed herself a smile. Her zygomatic activation was genuine but her orbicularis oculi — the muscle around the eyes that distinguishes a real smile from a performed one, the muscle that cannot be consciously controlled, the muscle that tells me everything — contracted at only 40 percent of her baseline for authentic positive affect. She was glad to see him. She was not as glad as her face suggested. The delta between those two truths is the space in which this entire story takes place.

"Nice chairs," she said.

"I was going for *interrogation room meets group therapy*."

"You nailed group therapy."

"That's worse, isn't it."

"Much worse."

They laughed. Desh's laugh: 187 hertz fundamental frequency, approximately 35 hertz
